disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by at least one full manic episode, often accompanied by major depressive episodes, in which mood disturbances are severe enough to cause marked impairment in social or occupational functioning or require hospitalization. Psychotic features (delusions and/or hallucinations) occur during mood episodes and are typically mood-congruent, although they can be mood-incongruent, which may complicate the differential diagnosis with primary psychotic disorders. The course is usually recurrent, with periods of relative euthymia between episodes, and episodes can be precipitated or unmasked by stress, sleep disruption, or substance use but are not solely caused by them. Distinguishing features from unipolar depression and cyclothymia include a history of clear-cut mania, duration and intensity of mood elevation, and the temporal relationship between psychosis and mood symptoms.

narrative.stressor: Chung had recently been promoted to lead a high-visibility, multi-million-dollar technology rollout, a role he saw as the culmination of years of meticulous career planning. In the months leading up to the project’s launch, he pushed himself harder than usual—working late nights, stacking multiple side certifications on top of his day job, and treating his sleep, diet, and workouts as optimization variables rather than limits, all while brushing off his parents’ and sister’s concerns about his health. As the go-live date approached, his behavior at work became increasingly erratic: he abruptly overrode team input, made risky unilateral decisions outside established protocols, and began insisting on unconventional data-driven "strategies" that alarmed colleagues and led to complaints to HR when a client meeting went off the rails. The crisis point came when he was escorted from the office after showing up to a steering-committee meeting in an agitated and disorganized state; his manager and a close coworker convinced him to go to the emergency department for an urgent psychiatric evaluation after he refused to step back from his responsibilities despite obvious functional decline.
narrative.chief_complaint: “For the last few weeks I’ve just been on this intense high, like I’m wired all the time and can’t turn it off, and it’s starting to scare people at work.”

narrative.stressor: Allison’s symptoms began to noticeably worsen during a period when she was juggling multiple family obligations: her adult daughter moved back home after a divorce, and her elderly mother’s health declined, leaving Allison coordinating appointments and finances on top of full-time warehouse shifts. Initially she coped by tightening her routines—color-coding bills, batch-cooking, and spending evenings knitting to unwind—but over several weeks her usual steadiness gave way to dramatic swings in energy and mood that her husband and daughter found increasingly unpredictable. She started missing volunteer commitments at the food pantry, stopped attending church regularly, and her reliability at home and at work deteriorated enough that her supervisor quietly pulled her aside about mistakes in inventory counts and erratic attendance. After a particularly tense family argument in which her behavior frightened her daughter and she admitted she no longer felt like herself, her husband and pastor encouraged her to see their primary care doctor, who, concerned about the intensity and duration of her mood changes and their impact on home and work life, referred her urgently to psychiatry.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My sleep has been completely off for weeks—either I’m up most of the night with my mind going or I crash and still wake up feeling worn out.”

narrative.stressor: Dennis had been angling for a district-manager promotion when his big-box retail chain announced a restructuring that eliminated several mid-level positions and shifted him to a less stable, commission-heavy role. The uncertainty about his future, combined with feeling passed over despite years of solid sales, unsettled his usual laid-back equilibrium, and friends at the coffee shop noticed sharper mood shifts and uncharacteristically intense rants about corporate politics. Over a few weeks, his functioning dropped off markedly—he began missing shifts, abandoned woodworking orders he had promised to friends, and stopped showing up to fishing club outings, while his apartment grew cluttered and bills went unpaid. The turning point came when his sister, who lived an hour away, drove down after his manager called her about his erratic behavior on the sales floor and found him in clear distress; realizing he could no longer manage work or daily responsibilities safely, she brought him to a community mental health clinic, where he was referred for urgent psychiatric assessment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since they changed my job around, I’ve sunk into this deep, heavy sadness that I just can’t shake, and it’s getting harder to do anything.”
